unit.name: When fine-tuning is and is not worth it
unit.description: Summarizes the instructor's caution against fine-tuning, including data, cost, overfitting, model-update risks, and narrow cases where fine-tuning can still make sense.
unit.summary: After exhausting prompt engineering, fine-tuning is framed as modifying model weights rather than changing the prompt context [ts=2479s]. The instructor argues against routine fine-tuning because it often requires substantial labeled data, can overfit to specific data, and may reduce general-purpose utility [ts=2497s]. The main practical objection is that fine-tuning is time- and cost-intensive, while the next foundation model may outperform the fine-tuned older model by the time work is complete [ts=2535s]. Fine-tuning can still make sense for repeated high-precision outputs or when a general model consistently fails at domain-specific language [ts=2570s]. A Slack fine-tuning example illustrates the risk: a model trained on company Slack behavior copied workplace conversational habits instead of following a request to write a blog post [ts=2592s].

key_points.text: Fine-tuning modifies model weights, whereas prompting and few-shot examples do not.
Fine-tuning typically requires substantial labeled data for the target task.
Fine-tuned models can overfit and lose general-purpose utility.
A new base model may outperform a fine-tuned older model before the fine-tuning effort pays off.
Fine-tuning remains plausible for repeated high-precision outputs or persistent domain-language failures.
The Slack example shows a model learning to behave like company messages rather than satisfying the requested task.
